source_text: Nunc ad diuina testimonia transeamus. sed prius unum proferam, quod est simile diuino et ob nimiam uetustatem et quod is quem nominabo ex hominibus in deos relatus est.. apud Ciceronem U. Cotta pontifex disputans contra Stoicos de religionibus et uarietate opinionum quae solent esse de diis, ut more Academicorum omnia faceret incerta, quinque fuisse Mercurios ait et enumeratis per ordinem quattuor quintum fuisse eum a quo sit Argus occisus; ob eamque causam in Aegyptum profugisse atque Aegyptiis leges ac litteras tradidisse. hunc Aegyptii Thoyth appellant, a quo apud eos primus anni sui mensis id est September nomen accepit. idem oppidum condidit, quod etiam nunc graece uocatur Mercurii ciuitas, et Pheneatae colunt eum religiose. qui tametsi homo fuit, antiquissimus tamen et instructissimus omni genere doctrinae adeo, ut ei multarum rerum et artium scientia Trismegisto cognomen inponeret. hic scripsit libros et quidem multos ad cognitionem diuinarum rerum pertinentes, in quibus maiestatem summi ac singularis dei asserit isdemque nominibus appellat quibus nos dominum et patrem. ac ne quis nomen eius requireret, άνώνυμον esse dixit, eo quod nominis proprietate non egeat, ob ipsam scilicet unitatem. ipsius haec uerba sunt: o se Oso; είς, b δὲ είς όνόματος ou προσδέεται έστι ykp o wv ὰνώνυμος. deo igitur nomen (non) est, quia solus est, nec opus est proprio uocabulo, nisi cum discrimen exigit multitudo, ut unam quamque personam sua nota et appellatione designes. deo autem, quia semper unus est, proprium nomen est deus. Superest de responsis sacrisque carminibus testimonia quae sunt multo certiora proferre. nam fortasse ii contra quos agimus nec poetis putent esse credendum tamquam uana fingentibus nec philosophis, quod errare potuerint, quia et ipsi homines fuerint. M. Varro, quo nemo umquam doctior ne apud Graecos quidem uixit, in libris rerum diuinarum quos ad C. Caesarem pontificem maximum scripsit, cum de quindecimuiris loqueretur, Sibyllinos libros ait non fuisse unius Sibyllae, sed appellari uno nomine Sibyllinos, quod omnes feminae uates Sibyllae sint a ueteribus nuncupatae uel ab unius Delphidis nomine uel a consiliis deorum enuntiandis. atouq enim deos, non Osouc, et consilium non βουλήν, sed βούλλαν appellabant Aeolico genere sermonis. itaque Sibyllam dictam esse quasi θεοβούλην. ceterum Sibyllas decem numero fuisse, easque omnes enumerauit sub auctoribus qui de singulis scriptitauerint. primam fuisse de Persis, cuius mentionem fecerit Nicanor, qui res gestas Alexandri Macedonis scripsit; secundam Libyssam, cuius meminerit Euripides in Lamiae prologo; tertiam Delphida, de qua Chrysippus loquatur in eo libro quem de diuinatione conposuit; quartam Cimmeriam in Italia, quam Naeuius in libris belli Punici, Piso in annalibus nominet; quintam Erythraeam, quam Apollodorus Erythraeus adfirmet suam fuisse ciuem eamque Grais Ilium petentibus uaticinatam et perituram esse Troiam et Homerum mendacia scripturum; sextam Samiam, de qua scribat Eratosthenes in antiquis annalibus Samiorum repperisse so scriptum; septimam Cumanam nomine Amaltheam, quae ab aliis Herophile uel Demophile nominetur, eamque nouem libros attulisse ad regem Tarquinium Priscum ac pro iis trecentos philippeos postulasse regemque aspernatum pretii magnitudinem derisisse mulieris insaniam; illam in conspectu regis tris combussisse ac pro reliquis idem pretium poposcisse; Tarquinium multo magis insanire mulierem putauisse; quae denuo tribus aliis exustis cum in eodem pretio perseueraret, motum esse regem ac residuos trecentis aureis emisse; quorum postea numerus sit auctus, Capitolio refecto, quod ex omnibus ciuitatibus et Italicis et Graecis praecipueque Erythraeis coacti adlatique sunt Romam cuiuscumque Sibyllae nomine fuerunt; octauam Hellespontiam in agro Troiano natam, uico Marmesso circa oppidum Gergithium, quam scribat Heraclides Ponticus Solonis et Cyri fuisse temporibus; nonam Phrygiam, quae uaticinata sit Ancyrae; decimam Tiburtem nomine Albuneam, quae Tiburi colatur ut dea iuxta ripas amnis Anienis, cuius in gurgite simulacrum eius inuentum esse dicitur tenens in manu librum. arum onmium Sibyllarum carmina et teruntur et habentur, praeterquam Cymaeae, cuius libri a Romanis occultantur nec eos ab ullo nisi a quindecimuiris inspici fas habent. et sunt singularum singuli libri: quos, quia Sibyllae nomine inscribuntur, unius esse credunt, suntque confusi nec discerni ac suum cuique adsignari potest nisi Erythraeae, quae et nomen suum uerum carmini inseruit et Erythraeam se nominatuiri praelocuta est, cum esset orta Babylone. sed et IlOS confuse Sibyllam dicemus, sicubi testimoniis earum ruent abutendum. omnes igitur hae Sibyllae unum deum praedicant, maxime tamen Erythraea, quae celebrior inter ceteras ac nobilior habetur, siquidem Fenestella diligentissimus scriptor de quindecim uiris dicens ait restituto Capitolio rettulisse ad senatum C. Curionem consulem, ut legati Erythras mitterentur, qui carmina Sibyllae conquisita Romam deportarent: itaque missos esse P. Gabinium M. Otacilium L. Valerium, qui descriptos a priuatis uersus circa mille Romam deportarunt. idem dixisse Varronem supra ostendimus. in his ergo uersibus quos Romam legati adtulerunt de uno deo haec sunt testimonia: εἷς θεός, ὂς μόνος ἄρχει, ὐπερμεγέθης ἀγένητος. hunc esse solum summum deum, qui caelum fecerit luminibusque distinxerit: ἀλλὰ θεὸς μόνος εἶς πανυπέρτατος, ὃς πεποίηκεν οὐρανὸν ἡέλιὸν τε καὶ ἀστέρας, ἠδέ σελήνην, καρποφόρον γαῖαν τε καὶ ὕδατος οἴδματα πόντου. qui quoniam solus sit aedificator mundi et artifex rerum uel quibus constat uel quae in eo sunt, solum coli oportere testatur: αὐτὸν τὸν μόνον ὄντα σέβεσθ᾽ ἡγήτορα κόσμου. ὃς μόνος εἰς αἰῶνα καὶ ἐξ αἰῶνος ἐτύχθη. item alia Sibylla quaecumque est cum perferre se ad homines uocem dei diceret, sic ait:
pass_a_gloss: Now let us proceed to divine testimonies. But first, I will bring forth one thing, which is similar to the divine and because of its great antiquity and because the one I will name was transferred from men to gods among the gods. In Cicero, U. Cotta, a pontiff, discussing against the Stoics about religions and the variety of opinions that are accustomed to be about the gods, so that, in the manner of the Academics, he might make all things uncertain, says that there were five Mercurys and, having enumerated four in order, the fifth was the one by whom Argus was killed; and because of this cause, he fled to Egypt and handed over laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call this one Thoyth, from whom the first month of their year, that is, September, received its name. The same one founded a city, which is even now called the city of Mercury in Greek, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Who, although he was a man, was nevertheless most ancient and most instructed in every kind of doctrine, so much so that he was given the surname Trismegistus because of his knowledge of many things and arts. This one wrote books, and indeed many, pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God and calls him by the same names by which we call the Lord and Father. And lest anyone might seek his name, he said that it is anonymous, because it does not need the property of a name, on account of its unity. His words are these: 'O the one God; one, indeed, is the one who does not need a name, and he is anonymous.' Therefore, God does not have a name, because he is alone, nor is a proper word needed, except when a multitude demands distinction, so that you might designate each person by their own mark and appellation. But for God, because he is always one, 'God' is his proper name. It remains to bring forth testimonies that are much more certain from the sacred and Sibylline poems. For perhaps those against whom we are arguing do not think that poets should be believed, as if they were inventing vain things, nor philosophers, because they could have erred, since they also were men. M. Varro, than whom no one was ever more learned, not even among the Greeks, in the books of divine things that he wrote to C. Caesar, the pontifex maximus, when he was speaking about the quindecimvirs, says that the Sibylline books were not of one Sibyl, but were called by one name, Sibylline, because all women who were seers were called Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the counsels of the gods that were to be announced. For the Aeolians called the gods not 'Osouc' but 'theos', and counsel not 'βουλήν' but 'βούλλαν'. And so, the Sibyl was said to be, as it were, 'θεοβούλην'. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls, and he enumerated all of them under the authors who wrote about each one. The first was from Persia, whom Nicanor mentioned, who wrote about the deeds of Alexander the Macedonian; the second was Libyssa, whom Euripides remembered in the prologue of Lamia; the third was Delphid, about whom Chrysippus spoke in that book that he composed about divination; the fourth was Cimmerian in Italy, whom Naevius named in the books of the Punic War, and Piso in the annals; the fifth was Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirmed was his fellow citizen and who prophesied to the Greeks who were going to Troy that Troy would perish and that Homer would write falsehoods; the sixth was Samian, about whom Eratosthenes wrote in the ancient annals of the Samians; the seventh was Cumana, named Amalthea, who was also called Herophile or Demophile by others, and who brought nine books to King Tarquin the Elder and asked for three hundred philippeos for them, and when the king scorned the magnitude of the price and ridiculed the woman's insanity, she burned three of them and asked for the same price for the remaining ones; Tarquin, thinking the woman was even more insane, was moved when she burned three more and persevered in the same price, and he bought the remaining ones for three hundred gold pieces; and afterwards, their number was increased when the Capitol was rebuilt, and they were brought from all the cities, both Italian and Greek, especially from Erythrae, to Rome, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were; the eighth was Hellespontian, born in the Trojan field, in the village Marmessus, near the city Gergithium, whom Heraclides of Pontus wrote was contemporary with Solon and Cyrus; the ninth was Phrygian, who prophesied in Ancyra; the tenth was Tiburtine, named Albunea, who is worshiped as a goddess in Tibur, near the banks of the river Anio, and whose image is said to have been found in the whirlpool, holding a book in her hand. And the poems of all the Sibyls are both worn out and preserved, except for those of the Cumana, whose books are hidden by the Romans and it is not lawful for anyone to inspect them except the quindecimvirs. And there are individual books of each one: which, because they are inscribed with the name of the Sibyl, are believed to be of one Sibyl, and they are confused and cannot be discerned or assigned to each one, except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into her poem and proclaimed that she was called Erythraean, since she was born in Babylon. But we will also call the Sibyl confused, wherever we will use their testimonies. Therefore, all these Sibyls proclaim one God, especially the Erythraean, who is considered more famous and noble among the others, since Fenestella, a most diligent writer, says that when the Capitol was restored, C. Curio, the consul, reported to the senate that legates should be sent to Erythrae to bring back the poems of the Sibyl that had been found: and so, P. Gabinius, M. Otacilius, and L. Valerius were sent, who brought back to Rome about a thousand verses that had been written by private individuals. Varro also said the same thing above. In these verses, therefore, that the legates brought to Rome, there are these testimonies about one God: 'One God, who alone rules, immense, ungenerated.' That this one is the only highest God, who made the heaven and distinguished it with lights: 'But God alone is one, most high, who made the heaven, the sun, and the stars, and the moon, and the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea.' Who, since he is alone the builder of the world and the artisan of things, either which consist in it or which are in it, testifies that he alone should be worshiped: 'Honor the one who is the only ruler of the world.' 'Who alone is from eternity and to eternity.' Likewise, another Sibyl, whoever she is, when she says that she brings the voice of God to men, says thus:

pass_b_english: Let us now turn to the divine testimonies. First, however, I will bring forward one figure who resembles the divine — on account of his immense antiquity and because the man I shall name was reckoned among the gods. In Cicero, the pontiff U. Cotta, arguing against the Stoics about religion and the variety of opinions concerning the gods, attempts, after the manner of the Academics, to render everything uncertain. He says there were five Mercuries; having enumerated four in order, he identifies the fifth as the one by whom Argus was slain, and adds that on this account he fled to Egypt and gave laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call him Thoyth, from whom the first month of their year — that is, September — took its name. This same figure founded a city that is still called in Greek the City of Mercury, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Although he was a man, he was the most ancient and the most thoroughly instructed in every kind of learning, so that his knowledge of many matters and arts earned him the surname Trismegistus. He wrote many books pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God and addresses him by the same names we use for the Lord and Father. And lest anyone seek his name, he declared it to be anonymous — because it does not need the property of a name, owing to its very unity. His words are these: "O the one God; one, indeed, is the one who does not need a name, and he is anonymous." Therefore God does not have a name, because he is alone; nor is a proper title needed, except when a multitude demands distinction so that each person may be designated by his own mark and appellation. But for God, since he is always one, "God" is his proper name.

It remains to produce testimonies that are far more certain, drawn from the sacred and Sibylline poems. For perhaps those against whom we contend do not think poets should be believed, as if they invent empty fictions; nor philosophers, since they could have erred, being themselves men. M. Varro — than whom no one more learned ever lived, not even among the Greeks — in his books on divine matters addressed to C. Caesar the pontifex maximus, when discussing the quindecimvirs, says that the Sibylline books were not the work of a single Sibyl, but were called by one name, "Sibylline," because all women prophets were called Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the announcing of the counsels of the gods. For the Aeolians called the gods not "Osouc" but "theos," and counsel not "boule" but "boulian." Hence the Sibyl was said to be, as it were, "theoboulia" — the counsel of God. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls, and Varro enumerates them all under the authors who wrote about each. The first was the Persian Sibyl, mentioned by Nicanor, who wrote the deeds of Alexander of Macedon. The second was the Libyan Sibyl, whom Euripides recalls in the prologue to the Lamia. The third was the Delphic Sibyl, of whom Chrysippus speaks in his book on divination. The fourth was the Cimmerian Sibyl in Italy, named by Naevius in his books on the Punic War and by Piso in his annals. The fifth was the Erythraean Sibyl, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirms was his fellow citizen; she prophesied to the Greeks sailing for Troy that Troy would perish and that Homer would write falsehoods. The sixth was the Samian Sibyl, about whom Eratosthenes writes in the ancient annals of the Samians that her writings were found. The seventh was the Cumaean Sibyl, named Amalthea, also called Herophile or Demophile by others. She brought nine books to King Tarquin the Elder and asked three hundred philippeos for them; the king scorned the price and mocked the woman's madness. Whereupon she burned three of the books and demanded the same price for the remaining six. Tarquin, thinking her even more insane, was moved when she burned three more and persisted at the same price, and he bought the remaining three for three hundred gold pieces. Afterwards their number was increased when the Capitol was rebuilt, and books were brought to Rome from all cities, Italian and Greek, especially from Erythrae, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were. The eighth was the Hellespontine Sibyl, born in the Troad, in the village of Marmessus near the city of Gergithus; Heraclides of Pontus writes that she lived in the times of Solon and Cyrus. The ninth was the Phrygian Sibyl, who prophesied at Ancyra. The tenth was the Tiburtine Sibyl, named Albunea, worshiped as a goddess at Tibur near the banks of the river Anio; her image is said to have been found in the whirlpool holding a book in her hand. The poems of all these Sibyls are both worn and preserved, except those of the Cumaean, whose books the Romans keep hidden, and it is not lawful for anyone but the quindecimvirs to inspect them. There are individual books for each Sibyl, but because they are inscribed with the name "Sibyl," they are believed to be the work of a single Sibyl; they are confused and cannot be discerned or assigned to each one, except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into her poem and declared beforehand that she would be called Erythraean, though she was born in Babylon. We too will call the Sibyl "confused" wherever we must use their testimonies. All these Sibyls, therefore, proclaim one God — especially the Erythraean, who is more famous and more highly regarded among the others. Fenestella, a most diligent writer on the fifteen men, says that when the Capitol was restored, the consul C. Curio reported to the senate that envoys should be sent to Erythrae to bring back the poems of the Sibyl that had been discovered. Accordingly P. Gabinius, M. Otacilius, and L. Valerius were sent; they brought to Rome about a thousand verses transcribed from private collections. Varro also said the same thing above. In these verses, then, that the envoys brought to Rome, we find these testimonies concerning one God: "One God, who alone rules, immense, unbegotten." That this one is the only supreme God, who made the heaven and distinguished it with lights: "But God alone is one, most high, who made the heaven, the sun, and the stars, and the moon, and the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea." He testifies that he alone ought to be worshiped, since he alone is the builder of the world and the artificer of all things, whether of those of which it consists or those that are in it: "Honor the one who is the only ruler of the world." review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex historical and mythological narrative regarding Hermes Trismegistus and the ten Sibyls. All Greek quotations and their Latin contexts are preserved with fidelity in both Pass A and B. The distinction between the 'confused' nature of the Sibylline books and the specific Erythraean Sibyl is correctly maintained. No omissions or additions were noted.
